title: Partial degradation & SLA playbook discovery with Cobalt Therapeutics
summary: Discovery focused on how Redwood handles partial degradation scenarios, multi-region failover, SLA expectations, and playbooks for graceful fallback. Customer asked about hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs for regulated clinical workload and auditability.
action_items: Samantha Li | Send tailored SLA one-pager and sample playbook (canary + regional fallback) | 2025-10-14
Ravi Patel | Share benchmark checklist and request: 48-hour traffic trace + sample prompts | 2025-10-13
Marta Ruiz | Provide list of regulatory auditors and required retention windows | 2025-10-16
next_steps: Redwood to send SLA one-pager and playbook
Schedule a 60-min technical deep dive with Cobalt platform + security (tentative week of 10/20)
Customer to provide anonymized traffic traces for pilot sizing
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-10-09 14:30 PT | Duration: 46m | Attendees: Samantha (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Marta (CTO), Evan (Platform), Priya (MLOps), Liam (Security)

Auto-summary: Quick discovery on how Redwood would behave under partial infra failures and what the escalation/playbook looks like. Also clarifying hosted vs dedicated vs private for PII and audit needs.

[00:00] Samantha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Samantha from Redwood. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Marta: Marta here, CTO at Cobalt. Hi.
[00:11] Evan: Evan, platform.
[00:13] Priya: Priya, MLOps.
[00:16] Liam: Liam on security.
[00:18] Samantha: Great. Ravi, do you want to intro from an SE angle?
[00:22] Ravi: Yeah, hi all. I'll mostly cover failure modes, fallback policies, and what telemetry we expose. Quick note: we'll be a bit detailed on routing and metrics so feel free to interrupt.
[00:34] Marta: Perfect — main reason for this call is we have a clinical safety review next month and need to lock down how inference degrades gracefully. We need to answer: if a region loses capacity, how do requests failover, what SLOs remain, and what's the customer impact. Also, legal wants to know retention and auditability.
[00:52] Samantha: Totally, that's exactly the scope. Maybe to orient us: what's your current infra? Hosted cloud? On-prem? Mix?
[01:00] Evan: We're hybrid. Prod-in-cloud (us-west + eu-west), some on-prem for PHI pipelines. Currently using a mix of managed endpoints and self-hosted model servers. We do autoscaling but it's not great for bursty LLM workloads.
[01:16] Priya: Right, and for the clinical flows we need 99.9% availability for inference calls that feed triage. But non-critical features can accept slower responses or lower-quality models.
[01:27] Liam: For security, we need KMS integration, key rotation logs, and per-request audit trails retained for 7 years.
[01:35] Ravi: Understood. Let me quickly sketch how Redwood's control plane and runtime approach this, and then we'll map it onto your constraints.
[01:42] Ravi: (quick high-level) We run a smart routing layer that can route by policy — latency-first, cost-first, or region-prefer. For a given request, the system tries the primary pool; if capacity isn't available or latency SLO is missed, we can failover to a warm-standby pool in another region, or degrade the model (e.g., quantized variant) as a last resort.
[02:03] Priya: When you say 'degrade the model' — is that an automated step in the runtime or a configured policy per route?
[02:10] Ravi: It's policy-driven per route. You can configure precedence: 1) try primary model in same region, 2) if capacity-exhausted within X ms, route to dedicated reserved capacity, 3) if still failing, route to a cheaper quantized variant in another region, 4) if none available, return a graceful error with structured payload indicating degradation reason.
[02:31] Marta: How do you measure the SLO in those cases? Our legal team wants a clear definition of 'available'.
[02:36] Samantha: Great question. Our SLA is measured as successful token generation under the contracted latency boundary. For hosted customers we publish per-region uptime and per-route p99 latency metrics. For dedicated/private we can provide a contract with measurable latency percentiles and an uptime target tied to reserved capacity.
[02:53] Evan: So in a partial failure where you fall back to a different model, does the SLA still count as met?
[02:58] Ravi: It depends on the contract. By default we treat model-variant fallbacks as successful responses (so token generation occurred) but we surface a 'quality tag' in the trace. For SLA purposes customers can choose whether variant fallbacks count toward SLA. Many enterprise customers elect to count only same-variant, same-region responses for the strict SLA and use a separate 'best-effort' metric for fallbacks.
[03:22] Priya: That makes sense. We probably want strict SLA for clinical triage and best-effort for analytics.
[03:28] Marta: Walk us through an incident timeline. Suppose us-west goes offline, what's the sequence and expected customer-facing behavior?
[03:36] Ravi: Sure. Sequence: detection (probe or health check fails) -> smart-router marks pool unhealthy -> in-flight requests either finish if KV cache present, or are retried up to N times -> new requests follow policy and route to standby capacity. If standby is in eu-west you'll see ~60–120ms added latency on average depending on model size and cross-region networking. We'll also drop to a lower-precision variant if configured to preserve latency.
[03:58] Evan: 60–120ms seems optimistic — cross-region on heavy models tends to be higher in our infra. Are you assuming Redwood inter-region private network?
[04:06] Ravi: Good point. For hosted we use cloud backbone — typically multi-region is 70–200ms depending. For Dedicated with private peering we can often get lower. I wrote 60–120 as a best-case for smaller models.
[04:17] Liam: For regulated use we can't send PHI outside certain regions. How do you enforce residency?
[04:22] Samantha: We have region affinity policies. You can set per-route restrictions: deny cross-region fallback for routes marked as 'resident-only'. For those, fallback is limited to reserved capacity in-region or a failover that returns structured error.
[04:36] Priya: Is it possible to configure a staggered fallback: first try reserved in-region, then quantized in-region, then block?
[04:42] Ravi: Yes, precedence rules are flexible. You define ordered policies. Example: primary -> reserved in-region -> quantized in-region -> block. The orchestration engine evaluates them in order.
[04:53] Marta: Audit logs — we need per-request X, Y, Z (request id, model variant, route decisions, user id if present). Can we export those into our SIEM?
[04:59] Ravi: Absolutely — we stream structured telemetry and trace events to your preferred sink (S3, BigQuery, or SIEM). There's some sampling default for high-volume routes but we can set 100% for critical routes.
[05:12] Liam: Key management — HSM? KMS?
[05:15] Samantha: We support KMS integrations (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault) and HSM-backed options for Private deployments. Key rotation logs and access audits are available. For Hosted we can integrate customer-managed KMS for model keys.
[05:30] Priya: One quick question on the fallback being visible to the application — do you add a header or a structured field in the response? We need to surface it into our UI so clinicians know degraded mode is active.
[05:39] Ravi: We attach a metadata block: {model_variant: "x", route_status: "fallback", reason_code: "capacity:region", quality_score: 0.82}. It's JSON-in-response or sent as trace headers depending on your integration.
[05:53] Evan: For pilot sizing, what data do you need from us?
[05:56] Ravi: A 48–72 hour anonymized trace with request sizes, sequence length distribution, and p95 arrival rates. Also which routes are critical (strict SLA) vs best-effort.
[06:08] Marta: We'll provide that. Legal question: if Redwood has an outage that causes loss of data, what's liability?
[06:15] Samantha: High level: our contracts have liability caps and we provide data durability guarantees for audit logs and stored artifacts. For Private deployments the customer manages persistence. We'll follow up with legal on the exact language — I'll send the contract excerpt.
[06:27] Priya: How do you do traffic shaping during degraded states to preserve critical throughput?
[06:31] Ravi: We have priority queues per-token and per-route rate caps. You can mark tokens/requests with priority. During congestion we throttle best-effort traffic and reserve a fraction for strict-SLA routes.
[06:43] Marta: Would that require changes to our client SDK?
[06:46] Ravi: Minimal — we support request headers to set request priority, or you can configure token-level policies in the control plane so no SDK change for basic use.
[06:55] Liam: Any per-tenant isolation concerns in multi-tenant hosted? If neighbor noisy-ness occurs, how are we protected?
[07:02] Samantha: For hosted we do aggressive fair-sharing and autoscaling; noisy neighbor protections include per-account rate limits and circuit breakers. For strict isolation we recommend Dedicated or Private.
[07:13] Evan: Cost tradeoffs — if we reserve capacity in-region for strict routes, what's the typical uplift?
[07:20] Ravi: Reserved capacity has a monthly commit; uplift depends on GPU type and utilization — ballpark 2–3x the per-token hosted spot price but gives predictable latency and failure behavior. We can run a cost model once we have traces.
[07:33] Marta: Ok. Can we see an example playbook for a multi-region failover with communication steps for ops and customers?
[07:39] Samantha: Yes — we'll send a playbook template: detection thresholds, automated failover timeline, ops steps, customer communications, and post-incident checklist.
[07:49] Priya: On the topic of metrics, do you provide real-time routing reasons so we can aggregate how many requests hit fallback?
[07:55] Ravi: Yes, we expose per-route counters: fallback_count, fallback_latency, fallback_quality. They show up in the Console and via APIs.
[08:05] Evan: Competitors — we evaluated GoliathAI and CloudRunAI. Goliath had decent routing but awful observability; CloudRun had better peering options but no dedicated playbook. How do you compare?
[08:18] Samantha: We try to be opinionated on observability + flexible routing. Our differentiator is the combo of per-route policy precedence, integrated tracing, and private deployment options.
[08:30] Marta: A few edge questions: what about prefix cache (KV cache) consistency during failover? If we warm a KV cache in eu-west but it's slightly stale is that a problem for clinical decisions?
[08:43] Ravi: Cache semantics are pluggable. For critical workflows we recommend pinning model state to in-region caches and treating cross-region cache as read-only fallback with TTLs. We'll show the cache consistency configuration in the technical deep dive.
[08:58] Priya: Do you have runbooks for partial data-plane degradation where the control plane is fine but certain GPU pools unhealthy?
[09:05] Ravi: Yes — the runbook covers detection, circuit breaker triggering, re-routing to dedicated pools, and communications. We'll walk through a runbook in the next session.
[09:16] Marta: Sounds good. A couple of last things: retention windows for logs (we said 7 years), and legal will need sample audit exports.
[09:25] Samantha: We'll provide sample exported audit bundle and a retention config doc.
[09:30] Liam: For SOC/ISO artifacts, can you share your attestation?
[09:33] Samantha: Yes — we'll attach SOC2 and the pen test summary in the follow-up package.
[09:38] Evan: Timeline: we want pilot-ready in ~6 weeks if contract ok. Is that feasible?
[09:43] Ravi: Feasible. Pilot: 2-week smoke + 2-week load + 2-week evaluation. With traces, we can size Dedicated and spin up pilot pools quickly.
[09:53] Marta: Great. Thanks.
[09:55] Samantha: Quick recap then — action items and next steps: send SLA one-pager, playbook, sample audit bundle, and benchmark checklist. Schedule deep-dive for week of 10/20. Anything else?
[10:09] Priya: We'll share traces and flags for strict routes.
[10:12] Liam: Legal will compile questions and we'll send to Samantha.
[10:15] Samantha: Awesome. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up by EOD with the doc links.

End of transcript. Notes: occasional mis-transcriptions: "KV cash" (should be KV cache) seen in auto-notes; speaker attribution may be slightly off in sections. Shared artifacts referenced: https://redwood.example.com/sla-playbook (SLA one-pager), https://drive.example.com/cobalt/trace-request-form, security pack link: https://redwood.example.com/security/soc2.zip
